1:
The two cities named in passing get more attention than the passing warrants. Gill and Clarke both report that Amphipolis was built by Cimon the Athenian, who sent ten thousand colonists to it, and that it took its name from the Strymon running on either side; Gill adds its older name of the Nine Ways and its present Turkish name, Barnes that the modern village on the site preserves a corruption of the ancient name. Ellicott places both cities on the great Roman road and recalls that Amphipolis was famous in the Peloponnesian War as the scene of the death of Brasidas, while Robertson traces that road from Byzantium to the Adriatic, over five hundred miles, an extension of the Appian Way. Ellicott then draws an inference from the distances: the two names mark the stages at which the travellers rested, and thirty Roman miles a day was their average rate, a toilsome journey for men so lately scourged.

Why nothing was attempted in either city divides the voices. Barnes reports the argument from the emphatic article before synagogue, that there was probably none at Amphipolis or Apollonia; Ellicott says simply that there was no Jewish population to give an opening; Robertson answers frankly that we do not know why Paul hurried through two such large cities, if he did, and that there are many gaps in Luke's narrative we have no way of filling. Henry and Calvin refer it instead to the guidance of the Spirit, who like the wind blows where he pleases, though they draw opposite conclusions from the silence: Henry supposes Paul stayed long enough to publish the gospel there notwithstanding, while Calvin suspects he did essay to do some good and, because it had no success, Luke passes it over. Chrysostom offers a third account, that they hastened past the small cities and pressed on to the greater, from which the word would flow as from a fountain into the towns around. Henry and Calvin agree at least on the courage of it, that after the shameful treatment at Philippi the opposition made him the more resolute, and Wesley notices something quite different in the wording: the narrative stops speaking of Paul's company as we at this point and does not resume until much later, from which he concludes that Luke was left behind at Philippi.

That Paul went first to the synagogue after saying he turned to the Gentiles is felt as a difficulty by both the Greek and the Genevan. Chrysostom answers that he did not leave them alone, such was his longing affection towards them, and cites the apostle's own wish for his brethren; Calvin answers that the harder sentence must be restrained to the company who had wickedly rejected the gospel, and marvels at a patience that entered again among men whose frowardness he had so often tried. Gill and Clarke say only that he constantly offered salvation to the Jews first. On the three sabbaths Ellicott finds a measure of the respect commanded by his character as a Rabbi, though he came with the marks of the scourge on him; Wesley notes that the days between are not excluded; Robertson argues at length that the three mark only the period of free access to the synagogue, and that the epistles imply a much longer stay, since he was helped more than once from Philippi and worked night and day to support himself. Calvin takes the phrase about disputing out of the Scriptures as the whole rule of the matter, that in the doctrine of faith the authority of God alone must reign.
3:
Two words describe the method, and the voices divide the labour between them. Barnes takes the first of unfolding what is shut or obscure and the second of laying down a proposition; Robertson turns it into a phrase, that Paul was not only expounding the Scriptures but propounding his doctrine alongside them, and cannot refrain from adding that such exposition as this would lead to more opening of mind and heart. Clarke sets out the procedure in two steps, collecting the scriptures that spoke of the Messiah and then applying them to Jesus, by which he corrected their notion of a triumphant Messiah and removed the scandal of the cross. Barnes and Ellicott both press that the article should be kept, the Christ, meaning the Messiah every Jew was expecting but none would recognise in a crucified man. Calvin frames it as three questions, whether he be, who he is and what he is, and observes that among Gentiles the apostle would have had to begin farther back, since profane men do not conceive that they need a Mediator at all, whereas among Jews that point was settled and could be passed over as superfluous. Ellicott adds that in the intervals between the sabbaths he worked as usual for his livelihood.

On those who believed, Barnes and Clarke agree that the devout Greeks were proselytes of the gate, who had renounced idols and lived a moral life without being circumcised; Ellicott reports that some good manuscripts divide them, reading devout persons and Greeks, and holds the Thessalonian church predominantly Gentile with some won from idolatry without passing through Judaism at all; Robertson explains their readiness by their being less under the control of the rabbis. Calvin reads the disproportion as a first token of the blindness the prophets had denounced, only a few Jews believing while a great multitude who stood farther off came in, and yet as proof that the covenant was not void, since the sparkles of election shine in the remnant; he insists too that these did not subscribe with a cold consent but joined themselves as companions and drew on themselves the hatred of their nation. Wesley answers the freethinkers who observe that women are more religious than men and impute it to weakness of understanding: in a religion that means taking up the cross, he says, women lie under a natural disadvantage of courage, so that their embracing it was the stronger evidence of the power of him whose strength is perfected in weakness. Gill notes only that faith came by the word and was received in the love of it.

The rabble that was hired is described three ways. Clarke, following Hesychius and the Jewish use of the word for judges, takes them for a low kind of lawyers, pettifoggers without principle who fomented litigation, and thinks the Jews chose them precisely because they carried some juridical credit; a Latin version, he notes, renders it simply certain lawyers. Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take them instead for the loungers of the market-place, the standing material of any mob, Robertson calling them idlers and loafers after the word Plato used. Barnes objects that lewd is an unhappy translation, the word not being in the original; Ellicott defends it in its older sense of vile or worthless, and traces it back further to the plain meaning of the untaught layman. The verse also carries a textual dispute: Gill reports the Alexandrian copy, the Vulgate and the Syriac omitting the clause about unbelief, Ellicott finds both that clause and the envy wanting in different manuscripts, and Clarke judges the evidence strongest against both and would omit them, while Robertson expounds the jealousy at length as the jealousy of one order of preachers towards another.
6:
The title Luke gives the magistrates draws the longest note. Ellicott observes that the Greek word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament nor in any classical writer, and that Aristotle, whose survey well-nigh exhausts the official titles of Greek cities, does not give it, though he records an analogous one elsewhere; an inscription on an arch of the modern city, he says, shows it to have been a special title of Thessalonica, and it appears there were seven who bore it, as with the Archons at Athens. He adds that the same inscription carries names identical with those of converts in the apostolic history. Robertson puts the point more sharply still: the word used to be cited as an instance of Luke's blundering, and has since been found in seventeen inscriptions, five of them from Thessalonica, which he calls a fine illustration of the historical accuracy of Luke in matters of detail. The two describe the same arch differently, Ellicott as still spanning a street of the city, Robertson as preserved in a museum.

On the charge of having turned the world upside down Barnes notes only that the accusation of producing confusion and disorder has often been brought against the gospel since, and Clarke turns it into a boast, that this was the very character his own forefathers bore for preaching it through every part of the land. Calvin makes it the standing condition of the gospel, that the uproars Satan raises are imputed to it and the blame of tumults laid on modest teachers by the very men who procure them, and he refuses the obvious remedy: we are not to give place to slanders and false reports but to stand stoutly for the truth, ready to hear evil for things done well.

The second charge was treason, and the voices differ over what law was invoked. Ellicott takes it of the edict of Claudius, binding strictly only at Rome and in the colonies but showing the drift of imperial policy, and Robertson thinks rather of the older laws of treason; Barnes reports that the Roman people and after them the emperors would not suffer the name of king in a vanquished province except by permission. Clarke answers that the apostles did proclaim Jesus as king, which is true, but never insinuated that his kingdom was of this world, and Calvin that the Jews knew perfectly well a spiritual kingdom did the empire no injury and caught at the pretence only to load innocent men with the odium of the crime. Ellicott alone allows the charge a foothold, noting how prominent the kingdom of Christ and especially his coming as King had been in the teaching at Thessalonica, which may itself have furnished the materials of the accusation.

Barnes and Clarke agree that neither rulers nor people had any disposition to persecute, and that the magistrates showed their unwillingness by letting Jason go; Robertson explains their alarm differently, that to the crowd it meant revolution and to the politarchs a charge of complicity if they let it pass. What was then taken of Jason is disputed. Gill reads it as satisfaction given by the defence they made, whereby it appeared that their principles had no tendency to sedition, though he notes the Syriac and Arabic render it sureties; Clarke likewise takes it as enough for the present to prove the apostles upright and peaceable. Barnes reports two harder constructions, that the pledge was that they should leave the city, or that Jason would harbour them no more but deliver them up if they returned. Ellicott and Robertson both take it as a formal bail in the legal sense, and Robertson draws a consequence from it, that the condition was probably that Paul and Silas depart and not return, which would explain the apostle's own account of being hindered from revisiting them.
10:
Barnes and Clarke read the night journey simply as flight, undertaken once the foundation of a church had been laid and further machinations were feared. Henry will not leave it there: the command to flee from one city to another intends the flight not so much for safety as for the carrying on of the work, flee to another to preach there, and he adds that out of the eater came forth meat, the persecution meant to stop the gospel being overruled to further it. Calvin marvels instead at the constancy of a man who, after such experience of that nation's stubbornness, went straight into another synagogue, and notes that the brethren who sent them off adjoined themselves as voluntary companions to the danger. Ellicott observes that Timothy apparently stayed behind, partly to help the converts under their trials and partly to bring word of them, so that at Berea the two were alone. On the town itself the notices differ: Ellicott says the ancient name survives in the modern one and gives it twenty thousand inhabitants, Robertson makes it a place of some six thousand about fifty miles off, Clarke locates it near the birthplace of Alexander, and Barnes adds that a medal of Berea survives inscribed of the second Macedonia.

The word Luke uses of the Bereans then divides the commentary sharply, and Calvin stands alone. He refers the nobility not to the mind but to the nation, that is, to birth and family, and meets the argument that the comparative form implies a comparison with Thessalonica by answering that the idiom is common among the Greeks; besides, he says, principal women had already believed at Thessalonica, so the Bereans are not to be thought preferred on that score. Gill takes the comparison to hold between the Jews of the two cities and refers it expressly not to birth, lineage or descent but to minds, dispositions and manners. Barnes grants that the word literally means better born but says it is used here of a quality of heart, and calls willingness to examine a doctrine always the proof of an ingenuous disposition. Clarke says the same and reckons them a better educated and more polished people, citing the Jewish maxim that none is of a noble spirit who does not employ himself in the study of the law. Ellicott makes it the generous and loyal temper ideally supposed to belong to those of noble origin, and Wesley puts it in a sentence, that to be teachable in the things of God is true generosity of soul.

On what they actually did the voices are at one. Clarke numbers the stages: they heard attentively, received the doctrine with readiness when the evidence appeared sufficient, searched the Scriptures to see whether the promises and types answered to the person and sufferings of Jesus, and continued at it daily. Barnes notes that the daily searching proves they had the Scriptures in their possession, and that the apostles always claimed to be teaching what the Scriptures taught. Robertson explains the verb as sifting up and down, the exact research of a legal examination, and remarks that the Bereans, far from resenting a new interpretation, examined it for themselves. Ellicott holds the balance carefully: they came to the proofs with a temper predisposed to faith, yet did not take their own wishes or the apostle's assertions as sufficient ground for it. Gill enters the one caveat, that no man is naturally disposed to regard the gospel, there being a natural enmity in the mind against it.
12:
Barnes takes the result as the ordinary consequence of examination, that much is gained when men can be induced to look into the Scriptures at all, and that the most invariable cause of unbelief is the refusal to investigate them; Gill and Clarke say the same more briefly, that having heard and searched as they did they were not likely to be deceived. Calvin enters a structural caution, that the verse does not select a few out of those just spoken of, which would be absurd, but records that many more were added by their example. Who the honourable Greek women were is less agreed. Clarke thinks mere heathens are meant rather than proselytes, and that some of the chief families of the place were reached; Ellicott takes them for Gentile converts of the upper class, as at Thessalonica; Wesley says the women were followed by their husbands, while Robertson infers the opposite order, that Luke implies by his wording that the men also were Greeks of rank, though he does not say so.

The pursuit from Thessalonica draws out the strongest language. Barnes explains the verb as agitating a crowd the way wind agitates the sea, a figure common in the classics and in Scripture, and Robertson renders it more violently still, shaking the crowds like an earthquake and disturbing them like a tornado, adding that success at Thessalonica had given the rabbis confidence and that the attack was sharp and swift. Ellicott connects it with the apostle's own later verdict on those who forbade him to speak to the Gentiles. Calvin looks past the men altogether: it is not men that procure the war but Satan, the father of lying, who pricks forward those that are his and uses them as fans to raise sedition, and who will never cease to weary Christ's faithful servants by open war, secret lying in wait, or domestic combat.

Whether the departure involved a deception is disputed on all sides. The received rendering suggests a feint towards the sea, and Barnes denies flatly that any sleight is implied, the words meaning only that they took him as far as the coast. Clarke goes further and rejects the idea as needless: feints may be allowable where life is at stake, but there is no necessity for one here, and he takes it for granted that Paul went by sea. Ellicott reports that many of the better manuscripts read as far as the sea and finds presumptive evidence for a voyage in the fact that no intermediate places are named, as they had been on the outward journey, so that Paul rounded the promontory and entered by the port. Robertson alone leaves it open, noting that Paul may have taken ship at a nearer harbour, and reporting the contrary conjecture that he gave the Jews the slip by going the whole way overland when they expected him to sail. Ellicott adds the human note, that when the escort turned back Paul was, for the first time since his labours began, absolutely alone, and that his urgent message to come with all speed shows how he felt it; Robertson observes that Silas and Timothy staying behind would also screen the flight, since it was Paul's blood the Jews wanted and not theirs. On the city he reached, Barnes and Clarke give much the same account, the foundation by Cecrops, the name taken from the goddess to whom it was dedicated, and the first city built on a rock in the midst of a plain which the lower city afterwards covered; Clarke measures its circuit in its flourishing state at twenty-two Roman miles and reports everything now in ruin, and Barnes notes that this was Paul's first visit, and perhaps the first of any Christian minister, and that his success there was for some cause not great.
16:
That the city was full of idols the voices establish by piling up witnesses, and three of them reach independently for the same joke, that at Athens it was easier to meet a god than a man: Barnes gives it from Petronius alongside Pausanias, Lucian and Livy, Clarke gives the Latin and the Pausanias in Greek, and Henry quotes it too, adding that Athens had more idols than all the rest of Greece together and twice as many sacred feasts, and that after the empire became Christian the city remained incurably addicted to idolatry, no edict of the Christian emperors availing to root it out.

What Paul made of the place divides them. Ellicott is the most explicit: he looked on the Theseus and the friezes of the Parthenon as we look on them in a museum, but whatever sense of beauty in art he had, and it was probably weak in any case, was overpowered by horror that men should bow down to the work of their own hands; the beauty of form we admire in an Apollo or an Aphrodite would be to him, unveiled, a thing to shudder at, for he knew too well what that love of sensuous beauty had led to. Barnes records only the negative fact, that a city surpassing all others in architecture, science and art drew from him no word of admiration. Henry approves the silence outright: a scholar in love with the learning of the ancients would have thought himself happy there, but Paul, though bred a scholar, had learned to call it a vain thing and had other work to mind. Robertson leans the other way and grows eloquent over the Jew of Tarsus standing where Socrates had taught, near the Academy and the Lyceum, the Porch and the Garden, in what he calls the art centre of the world. Calvin turns the contrast into an argument: the city that was the mansion-house of wisdom, the fountain of arts and the mother of humanity exceeded all others in blindness, and the Lord suffered those masters of the liberal sciences to fall into an unwonted madness so that every age might learn what man's wit can do in matters that concern God. Chrysostom, reading forward, notices something else, that Paul met greater trials among the Jews than among the Gentiles, since at Athens the thing went as far as ridicule and there ended.

His going to the market-place is treated as the novelty it was. Wesley thinks he had no design of preaching at Athens at all, and that his zeal drew him into it unawares without waiting for his companions. Ellicott calls the third mode of action a new experiment: he had watched others disputing there of the highest good and the chief end of life, and asked why he should not take part and lead earnest inquirers to the truth they sought in vain. Robertson says he took his stand like Socrates before him and fell into conversation with whoever happened by, and reckons the audience more casual than a crowd stopping for street preaching, adding that the Painted Porch where Zeno had held forth stood over against the citadel, so that Paul may have stood near the spot. Barnes and Clarke describe the place as the resort of business and leisure alike, where philosophers were often found in public discussion. Gill, noting the synagogue, argues that Jews had long been settled at Athens and that this is how the philosophers came by their acquaintance with Jewish books, from which he thinks they borrowed much. Calvin dwells on the title given to the devout, that aptness to be taught is itself a beginning of faith and earns them an honourable name.
18:
On the two schools that encountered him the voices converge on one point: the founder is not to be judged by his followers. Clarke says the Epicureans certainly held that the gods governed nothing and that the chief good lay in the gratification of sense, but that it is not clear Epicurus himself maintained it; Barnes distinguishes the rational and regulated pleasure the founder meant from the voluptuousness into which the sect fell; Gill divides them outright into a strict sort who placed happiness in the pleasure of the mind arising from moral virtue and a loose sort who took their master grossly; Ellicott reports that the life of Epicurus seems to have been marked by generosity, self-control and even piety, but that where no law is written in the heart each man is left to judge what will please him most, and most men decide for ease. Of the Stoics, Wesley notes that they held matter eternal and all things governed by irresistible fate, Clarke that Seneca reckoned any good and wise man equal to Jupiter, and Robertson that the austerity of self-mastery Zeno taught ministered to pride, or to suicide when it failed. Calvin observes that the two sects, diametrically opposed, had each their own vices, the Epicureans being open enemies of the liberal arts. Wesley adds the shrewdest observation, that the apostle levels his discourse at the chief errors of both without expressly attacking either, simply by giving a plain summary of his own principles.

Clarke explains the word of contempt they threw at him as literally a collector of seeds, the name of a small bird that lives by picking them up on the road, and thence of a man who gathers the sayings of others without order or method; Wesley calls the sneer the language of natural reason, full of and satisfied with itself, and defends the other misunderstanding, that they took Jesus and the Resurrection for a god and a goddess, on the ground that the Athenians might as well count the resurrection a deity as shame and famine and many more.

Whether what followed was a trial is the chief question of the passage. Gill holds they did not lay hands on him by violence but invited him in a friendly manner to a place more convenient for hearing; Barnes finds no accusations, no witnesses and none of the forms of trial, and puts it down to the inquisitive spirit of a people willing to hear before condemning; Wesley says plainly that he does not appear to have been carried there as a criminal; Calvin argues that he was brought where the great assembly was, so that the disputation might be had before a famous audience, and adds that anywhere else it would have been a capital offence to gather a crowd and speak in a public place, but that at Athens the appetite for news secured a hearing even for triflers. Ellicott alone presses the other way: there would be no reason to take him to the Areopagus rather than elsewhere unless some trial were intended, and since a member of the Court was among the converts the Court was probably sitting, so that what happened was a preliminary inquiry without formal indictment and the speech an apology answering no distinct charge. Robertson takes a middle position, an examination whether the new teaching was legal but not a criminal trial, since the day for that had passed. He also doubts the familiar picture of Paul on the summit of the hill, there being no room there for a large gathering, and notes that the Court commonly met in a portico opening on the market-place.
20:
The request is polite, and the reason Luke gives for it is documented at length. Barnes and Clarke assemble almost the same battery of ancient witnesses to Athenian curiosity: Demosthenes on the men in the place of public resort asking whether there is any news, Thucydides on their excelling in suffering themselves to be deceived by novelty of speech, and the old scholiast whose comment on him nearly reproduces Luke's own words. Ellicott adds that Demosthenes reproached them with idling in the market asking what news there was of Philip while they should have been preparing to act, and that the same word for something newer is used elsewhere of the prattler who asks whether there is anything new and then whether there is anything newer still; the strangers present he takes for a motley group of young Romans finishing their education, artists and philosophers from every province. Robertson remarks that the new soon went stale with them, and Wesley that new things quickly grew cheap and they wanted those that were newer. Clarke turns the whole thing on his own century: the itch for news, he says, argues a worldly or unsettled mind, and is wonderfully prevalent in London, where even ministers of the gospel have become Athenians in this sense.

The word Paul opens with then divides the commentary. Barnes calls the received rendering a most unhappy translation, since the term properly means reverence towards the gods and is used by the classic writers in a good sense; Clarke gives it as an acknowledgment that they are greatly addicted to religious practices, and makes that the ground of his appeal for a candid hearing; Robertson calls it a neutral word used either way, reports the suggestion that Paul employs it with a kindly ambiguity, thinks it unlikely he would open by slapping his audience in the face, and observes that how one takes the adjective colours the whole speech. Calvin takes the opposite road: superstition is precisely the charge, the word signifying the immoderate fear with which superstitious men torment themselves, so that the Athenians are told they pass all measure. Gill notes only that he stood among the Areopagites and the philosophers together.

On the shape of what follows the accounts differ in emphasis rather than substance. Calvin divides it into five members: superstition charged, then who and what God is by natural argument, then the blockishness of men created to know their Maker and yet wandering in the dark, then the absurdity of figuring God by statue or picture when the mind of man is his true image, and at the last Christ and the resurrection. Henry frames it by contrast with the earlier sermons: with Jews the business was to open and allege that Jesus is the Christ, but with heathens it was to lead them by the common works of providence to the knowledge of the Creator, and he sets this discourse to the polite idolaters of Athens beside the earlier one to the rude idolaters of Lystra. Wesley finds the shape in their own appetite, that they inquired after new things and Paul began with the first things and went on to the last, both of which were new to them. Barnes observes that everything in it is calm, grave and argumentative, and that Paul neither denounced his hearers nor supposed that assertion would convince them, and Robertson that he speaks not as a man on trial but as one trying to get a hearing. Ellicott sets the scene, the Court sitting in the open air at the head of a flight of steps cut in the rock, with the temple of the Eumenides below him, the Theseum to the east, and the Parthenon facing him on the citadel.
23:
Ellicott grades the opening adjective more finely than the rest: it means fearful of the gods beyond others, and the apostle deliberately withholds the word the Athenians loved to use of themselves, which he keeps for those who worship the living God, choosing instead one that is neutral with a slight touch of disparagement; the opening words, he thinks, would gain and were perhaps meant to gain the ears of the philosophers. He fills out the type from an ancient portrait of the man who consults soothsayers, believes in omens, gives up a journey at the sight of a weasel on the road, and goes with wife and children to be initiated into the mysteries, and instances a general who countermanded a strategic movement because the moon was eclipsed.

On the altar itself the question is whether the apostle reported it fairly. Clarke passes on the charge, made long before him, that Paul found the inscription in the plural and quoted it in the singular so as not to seem to acknowledge many gods, and calls the suggestion a most foolish saying, since such a begging of the question would have wrecked his defence before intelligent judges. Calvin rejects the same charge on quite different ground, that the inscription was in every man's mouth so that there was no room for craft, and that the matter itself required the singular. Robertson notes independently that an ancient traveller does speak of altars to gods unknown in the plural at Athens. Who raised it, and to whom, is answered three ways. Wesley reports the supposition that Socrates set it up to express covertly his devotion to the only true God while deriding the plurality of the others, and the further supposition that it honoured the God of Israel, who had no image and whose name was never made known to the Gentiles; Clarke reports the same Jewish view, that the ineffable name made him the anonymous god. Robertson gives an account owing nothing to either, that in a pestilence a sheep was to be sacrificed to the befitting god whoever he might be, since an altar dedicated to the wrong deity would provoke the anger of the rest. Barnes and Clarke both cite the same ancient oath, sworn by the unknown God at Athens, though under different authors' names.

Calvin raises the hardest question here himself: how can the apostle allow that they worshipped at all, when God refuses every worship not agreeable to his word, and Christ condemned the Samaritans for worshipping what they knew not though they boasted of the God of Abraham? His answer is the principle he finds governing the whole speech, that God cannot be rightly worshipped until he is first made known, so that the definition of God must come before the manner of worshipping him; and with profane men, he notes, the proofs had to be drawn from nature itself, since citing Scripture to them would have been in vain. Gill and Clarke both hear the opening article as a double stroke, against the Epicureans who made the world a fortuitous concourse of atoms and against those who held matter eternal, Gill naming the Aristotelians and observing that men of both sects were doubtless present. Barnes reads the whole design as a proof of the folly of idolatry meant to lead them to repentance. On the clause about temples Ellicott makes the finest observation of the passage: the thought is the one the persecutor had heard from Stephen, which had then driven him to fanaticism when it was asserted of the temple at Jerusalem, and which he now extends to every temple raised by hands; Robertson adds that Paul may well have pointed to the Parthenon as he said it.
25:
That God is served by no hands and needs nothing is pressed against a particular error. Barnes finds behind it the heathen notion that the gods are fed by the offerings made to them, and sets against it the psalm in which God says that if he were hungry he would not tell us. Clarke calls it an indirect stroke against images and sacrifices alike. Ellicott observes that both schools present would have accepted so much, and quotes a Latin poet of the Epicurean persuasion on a divine nature strong in itself, needing nothing of ours, neither won by gifts nor moved by wrath; Robertson agrees the self-sufficiency of God was taught in those schools, but says the Epicurean missed it by putting God outside the universe. Calvin turns the objection on his own side: may not the same charge fall on the ceremonies of the law? He answers that the faithful never placed the worship of God in them but counted them helps to their infirmity, whereas the Gentiles reckoned that images and incense discharged the offices of godliness outright, a folly their own poets derided. Wesley notices that the clauses answer term for term to what follows about living and moving and being.

The unity of the race is asserted next, and here the text itself is disputed. Clarke reports the word blood omitted by leading manuscripts, by several versions and by early writers, and Robertson calls it a later explanatory addition; Gill keeps it, noting only that the Vulgate reads of one and the Arabic of one man. Clarke shows the word was in any case commonly used for race and stock, and sets against the doctrine the Athenian conceit of being self-produced aboriginals, mocked in antiquity with the gibe that the first men sprang up in Attica like radishes; Robertson notes the same claim, and adds that the cosmopolitanism here rises above both Greek exclusiveness and Jewish pride. Ellicott calls this the apostle's philosophy of history and observes how little a Greek was likely to accept it, the distinction between Greek and barbarian being for him radical and the one meant by nature to serve the other. Barnes draws a nearer conclusion, that no part of the race has any right to enslave or oppress another on account of a difference of complexion. Calvin adds that the variety of religions is therefore a corruption, since a common origin should have been a bond of consent.

The end of it all is that they should seek and grope. Clarke renders the verb of a blind or blindfolded man feeling his way, and Robertson likens it to feeling along the walls of a darkened room for the door, reporting that Helen Keller, when first told of God, said she had known of him already, groping in the dark after him. Ellicott presses the doubting particle strictly, as implying the end was not reached, the altar to the Unknown being itself the witness. Barnes holds it was possible to find God from his works though with difficulty, which makes idolatry both folly and wickedness; Calvin says God has engraven such manifest marks everywhere that even blind men may know them by groping, so that men are not merely blind but blockish; Wesley places feeling midway between seeking and finding, the lowest of the senses fitly answering to the lowest knowledge of God, and adds that God lays no force upon man. Gill notes only that the Creator and Benefactor who appointed their times and places should be sought for that reason.
28:
Ellicott parses the three verbs philosophically, the first of our animal life, the second not of bodily motion in space but of the emotional nature, since the ethical writers derived their word for the passions from it, and the third of that which constitutes our essential being, the intellect and will; what they express, he says, is not merely omnipresence but that the power for every act and thought comes from God. Robertson calls it real immanence and not Stoic pantheism, and reads the three as an ascending scale climaxing in bare existence. Calvin ranks them the other way, life being the most excellent, motion next and being least, and holds that the apostle put the highest first; he also keeps the preposition in rather than by, since to say we live in God has the greater force, and guards it at once against the trifling of brain-sick men who make all things full of gods. Gill adds that all motions of body and mind are of God, though their disorder is of ourselves. On the quotation Clarke observes that the words stand exactly in one poet and with a single letter altered in a hymn of another, and that by your own poets the apostle means Grecian poets rather than men born at Athens; Wesley makes the poet an Athenian of three hundred years before, while Robertson names him a man of Cilicia, and adds that the apostle knew perfectly well the line was written of Zeus and applied only the idea in it.

From the sonship the argument runs at once against images. Barnes and Clarke put it the same way: the parent must resemble the offspring, so that if we are living and intelligent the source of our being must be so too, and since it would be impious to worship a man, who is far more excellent than an image, it is worse to worship the image. Calvin sharpens it: the soul, in which the image of God is properly engraven, cannot itself be painted, so that it is more absurd still to paint God; and he presses the general doctrine that God is falsely transfigured whenever his majesty is represented by a visible shape. Wesley notes that the denial goes further than likeness, refusing these things any analogy at all by which they might represent him. Ellicott observes how differently the apostle speaks of idolatry from the older prophets, as one who has studied its genesis and can treat it with pity rather than scorn, and he hears in the three materials named the colossal gold of Phidias, the silver of famous shrines, and the marble quarried for Athens.

What the overlooking of the past means then divides them sharply. Gill takes it as contempt and indignation, God despising them for their folly and in evidence of it leaving them without revelation or prophets. Ellicott takes it as the thing in which the apostle found comfort, ignorance mitigating the guilt and therefore the punishment of the heathen world, and Barnes likewise as a passing over without coming forth to punish. Robertson denies both readings any warmth: the verb is merely negative, God had objected all along, and the received rendering wrongly suggests condoning, a suggestion Ellicott also thinks the English phrase carries too far. Calvin meets the objection that antiquity and common consent vouch for the old religions by answering that men never make an end of erring until God helps them, and refuses to say why he waited four thousand years, since where Scripture conceals the reason sobriety is worth more than preposterous wisdom. Wesley turns the command to repent against the audience: it declared universal guilt, confronted the pride of the haughtiest Stoic, and bore down the plea of fatality, since no one could repent of doing what he could not but have done.
31:
Ellicott hears the close as the audience would have heard it, a seeming relapse into the popular mythology which their own satirists said not even boys believed any longer; the Epicurean rejected divine government outright, and the Stoic held that the world's story was itself its judgment day and looked for no other. Barnes and Clarke both make the resurrection the seal on the claim, Barnes reasoning that God would not work a miracle in favour of an impostor. Calvin says the judgment is set before them to awake them from their dream, and that none are fit teachers of the gospel but those who are criers of the highest Judge. Cyril of Jerusalem, on the session at the right hand, gathers a chain of testimonies from the Gospel and the epistles. Wesley remarks how fitly this was said in their own supreme court, and adds that this was by no means all the apostle meant to say, the indolence of some hearers and the petulancy of others having cut him short. Robertson takes up the charge that Paul here abandoned the simple gospel for philosophy, and asks whether he did.

What broke the discourse off is agreed, and why is not. Clarke judges that Paul had not finished and was probably about to preach salvation through Christ crucified when the assembly instantly broke up, and Barnes too thinks the derision produced a disturbance that ended the speech, both comparing the interruption of Stephen. Robertson explains the offence: the Greeks believed the soul lived on but had no conception of a rising of the body, and had listened with respect until a resurrection was named as fact. Henry supplies the maxim of their schools, that from privation to possession there is no return and life once lost is irrecoverable, and notes that they had deified their heroes after death but never thought of their being raised. Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson divide the audience alike, the mockers being chiefly Epicureans, who denied a future state, and those who deferred being Stoics; Ellicott hears indignation in what follows, the apostle declining to stay and expose his Lord's name to the jests of scoffers, while Chrysostom asks rather why he was in such haste to leave a city where no danger threatened, and answers that he knew he would do them no great good and was being led to Corinth. Gill observes that his quiet departure shows he had not been tried.

Whether Athens was a failure divides them at the last. Henry says few were the better and the gospel had as little success there as anywhere; Calvin infers from the naming of one man and one woman that few believed at first, the rest remaining neither despisers nor disciples; Ellicott points the contrast with the great multitude at Thessalonica and Berea. Robertson answers that no sermon is a failure which brings a company of men to believe, and that many a grander sermon reaps no such harvest; Barnes holds the conversion of one man worth the labour. On the convert Clarke notes that none sat in that court who had not first been archon, and reports the conjectures that he became first bishop of Athens and that the woman was his wife, with the verdict that all this has little foundation; Ellicott dates the treatise on the heavenly hierarchy circulated under his name to some centuries later and observes that legend has since made him the patron saint of France; Wesley calls the writings spurious, fathered on him by men fond of high-sounding nonsense; Calvin says it is too gross to ascribe such books to him. Robertson alone repeats the tradition of his bishopric and martyrdom without comment.
